tagline: The first half of a two-volume history: the story of Jesus, Savior of the poor, the outsider, and the lost, told to a man named Theophilus so that he might know the certainty of what he had been taught.
overview:
Luke is the longest of the four Gospels and the first of two books by the same author; the second is the Acts of the Apostles. It opens with something none of the other Gospels has, a formal preface in polished Greek that explains the author's method: many have written accounts, the material was handed down by eyewitnesses, and he has investigated everything carefully in order to write an orderly account for “most excellent Theophilus” (1:3). Then the story begins in the temple in Jerusalem, with an old priest and a promise, and moves through the births of John the Baptist and Jesus, Jesus' ministry in Galilee, a long section on the road to Jerusalem, and his death, resurrection, and ascension.

Much of Luke's material appears in no other Gospel. Only Luke tells of the shepherds at the manger, the boy Jesus in the temple, the Good Samaritan, the lost coin and the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus in the tree, the thief on the cross who is promised paradise, and the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. These stories share a direction. The good news comes to the poor, the sick, women, Samaritans, tax collectors, and sinners, and it comes with joy. Jesus sums up his own mission near the end: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10).

Luke matters because it shows the story of Jesus as history that fulfills Israel's Scriptures and opens toward the whole world. It begins among faithful Jews waiting in the temple for the consolation of Israel and ends with the risen Jesus explaining that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled (24:44), and that repentance and forgiveness will be preached to all nations. Acts then tells how that happened. Between them the two volumes make up more than a quarter of the New Testament, more than any other single author contributed.
author:
The Gospel does not name its author, but the tradition that Luke wrote it is early and uniform, and no other name was ever attached to it. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 3.1.1, around AD 180) says Luke, the follower of Paul, set down in a book the gospel Paul preached, and in 3.14.1 he argues from the we passages of Acts that Luke was Paul's inseparable companion. The Muratorian fragment, a Latin list of accepted books, calls the third Gospel the work of Luke the physician, whom Paul took with him, and adds that Luke did not see the Lord in the flesh. It is usually dated to the late second century, though Albert Sundberg (1973) and Geoffrey Hahneman (1992) argued for the fourth. A Latin prologue to Luke, one of the so-called anti-Marcionite prologues, of disputed date, calls him a Syrian of Antioch and a physician who died unmarried at eighty-four in Boeotia.

Paul names Luke three times: “Luke, the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), a fellow worker (Philemon 24), and “Only Luke is with me.” (2 Timothy 4:11). Colossians 4:10-11 seems to list him apart from the coworkers who are Jewish, so many think Luke was a Gentile, though some dispute the inference. The strongest internal evidence is in Acts, where the narrative shifts without comment from they to we (16:10-17, 20:5-21:18, 27:1-28:16; Codex Bezae adds a we at Antioch in 11:28). The traditional reading is that the author was there. Others think he used a travel diary, his own or another's. Vernon Robbins (1978) proposed that first-person narration was a convention of ancient sea-voyage stories; Colin Hemer and Susan Marie Praeder, among others, doubted that such a convention existed. Philipp Vielhauer's essay on the Paulinism of Acts (1950) argued that the theology Acts gives Paul is too unlike his letters for a companion to have written it; defenders reply that a companion's portrait need not reproduce the letters' arguments.

The claim that medical vocabulary proves a physician wrote the book (W. K. Hobart, The Medical Language of St. Luke, 1882) was answered by Henry Cadbury (The Style and Literary Method of Luke, 1920), who showed that educated writers without medical training used the same words. The case now rests on the tradition and on Acts. Whoever he was, the author wrote the most literary Greek in the Gospels and knew the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) intimately.
date:
Luke was written before Acts, since Acts 1:1 refers back to it, so the two are dated together. Three positions have serious defenders.

An early date, before about AD 62, was argued by Adolf von Harnack (The Date of the Acts and of the Synoptic Gospels, 1911), John A. T. Robinson (Redating the New Testament, 1976), and Colin Hemer (1989). Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years (around AD 60 to 62) and says nothing of his death, Nero's persecution, or the fall of Jerusalem; on this view Luke stopped because events had reached his own day.

A date between about AD 75 and 90 is the majority view, held for example by Joseph Fitzmyer (about 80 to 85) and Raymond Brown. Its reasons are that Luke used Mark, usually dated to the late 60s or around 70, and that Luke's wording of Jesus' warning, “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies” (21:20), and of enemies building an embankment against the city (19:43), reads like knowledge of the Roman siege of AD 70. Defenders of the earlier date answer that the language draws on Old Testament siege oracles and that Acts may end where it does because Paul preaching unhindered in Rome is the goal of the story (28:31).

An early second-century date, around AD 110 to 125, is argued by Richard Pervo (Dating Acts, 2006) and Joseph Tyson (Marcion and Luke-Acts, 2006). Steve Mason (Josephus and the New Testament, 1992) argued that Luke-Acts shows knowledge of Josephus's Antiquities, finished in AD 93 or 94, pointing among other things to the order of Theudas and Judas in Acts 5:36-37; others find the parallels too general to prove dependence. The latest possible date is set by Marcion, who used a form of Luke by about AD 144, and by P75, a papyrus copy of Luke from around 200.
setting:
The story is set in Judea and Galilee under Roman rule, from the last years of Herod the Great (who died about 4 BC) to the governorship of Pontius Pilate (about AD 26 to 36). Luke anchors it in public history more carefully than any other Gospel writer. The birth is dated by the emperor Augustus and a census under Quirinius, governor of Syria (2:1-2), and John's preaching by the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with Pilate governing Judea, Herod Antipas ruling Galilee, and Annas and Caiaphas holding the high priesthood (3:1-2). The Jerusalem temple, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great, frames the book: it opens with Zechariah burning incense there and closes with the disciples praising God in its courts (24:53).

The first readers are harder to place. Theophilus has a Greek name meaning friend of God, and the title “most excellent” was used for men of rank, such as the governors Felix and Festus in Acts (23:26, 26:25). He may have been a patron who paid for the book's copying and circulation, a common practice for ancient authors, as Josephus dedicated his later works to one Epaphroditus, or a believer of standing who had been instructed in the faith. Beyond him the book seems written for a mainly Gentile church in a Greek-speaking city of the eastern empire, one that wanted to know how a movement born among Jews in Judea came to include people like them, and whether it could be trusted. Tradition has suggested Antioch, Achaia, and Rome; the book itself does not say.
purpose:
Luke states his purpose himself: he has written so that Theophilus may know the certainty of the things he has been taught (1:4). The book confirms faith by setting out what happened in order, grounded in eyewitness testimony. It also answers questions a Gentile church faced. Was this the continuation of Israel's faith or a new sect? Luke shows Jesus fulfilling God's promises to Israel and the inclusion of Gentiles planned from the start (2:32). Was it a threat to Roman order? Roman officials find no fault in Jesus (23:4, 23:14-15, 23:22) or, in Acts, in Paul. Who belongs? The poor, the sinful, and the outsider are welcomed, and the rich and respectable are called to repentance with everyone else.

The purpose runs across both volumes. Henry Cadbury's The Making of Luke-Acts (1927) established the habit of reading the two books as one work in two parts, and the evidence is strong: the same dedicatee, the summary of the first book at the start of the second (Acts 1:1-2), the ascension told at the end of one and the start of the other, and themes (the Spirit, prayer, witness, the nations, Jerusalem) that begin in the Gospel and are completed in Acts. Mikeal Parsons and Richard Pervo (Rethinking the Unity of Luke and Acts, 1993) accepted one author but questioned whether the books share one genre and one narrative design, and the church itself never copied them together: in the manuscripts Luke stands among the Gospels and Acts travels with the letters.
story: Luke picks up the Old Testament story where it paused. Its first chapters are full of the language of the Greek Old Testament: an old childless couple like Abraham and Sarah or Elkanah and Hannah, the angel Gabriel from Daniel, and songs that echo Hannah's prayer and the Psalms. The long silence after the prophets ends with John, who comes in the spirit and power of Elijah, as Malachi had promised. The Gospel then tells how God's promises to David and to Abraham are kept in Jesus, and it reaches further back than any other Gospel, tracing his line through David and Abraham to Adam, son of God (3:38). It ends where Acts begins, with the ascension and the command to wait in Jerusalem for power from on high. Acts carries the same story from Jerusalem to Rome, so that the two books together cover the arc from the temple in Jerusalem to the capital of the Gentile world. Hans Conzelmann (Die Mitte der Zeit, 1954; English 1960) described Luke's history as three periods, Israel up to John, the ministry of Jesus as the middle of time, and the age of the church; later scholars have questioned how sharply Luke divides them, but the book plainly sees itself as the hinge between Israel's Scriptures and the church's mission.
christ: Luke presents Jesus as Savior, a title the angels announce to shepherds (2:11) and one that Matthew and Mark never use. He is the Son of David who will reign forever, the Son of God conceived by the Holy Spirit, and the prophet anointed by the Spirit to preach good news to the poor. In his first sermon at Nazareth he reads from Isaiah 61, “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor” (4:18), and says the Scripture is fulfilled that day. Luke calls him Lord in the narrator's own voice, the title the Greek Old Testament uses for God, far more often than Matthew or Mark do. He also stresses that the Messiah's suffering was necessary: the risen Jesus explains to the Emmaus disciples, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, what was written in all the Scriptures about himself (24:27). And Luke's Jesus is the one who seeks the lost: he eats with sinners, forgives a criminal dying beside him, and prays for those who crucify him. The church confesses on this ground that Jesus is truly God and truly man, crucified for sinners, bodily raised (Luke insists he eats fish before the disciples, 24:42-43), and ascended to the Father.
reading:
Read Luke as an ancient history written by a believer, not a modern biography. Luke selects and arranges, sometimes by theme rather than strict chronology, and he often pairs a man and a woman (Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna, the shepherd with his sheep and the woman with her coin). Watch the meals, the prayers, and the word today. The central section (9:51-19:27) is framed as the road to Jerusalem, but it gathers teaching on discipleship, wealth, prayer, and the kingdom more than it logs a route.

Readers comparing Luke with Matthew and Mark will meet the Synoptic problem: the three share much wording and order, so one must have used another or a common source. The Two-Source hypothesis, formulated by Christian Hermann Weisse (1838) and H. J. Holtzmann (1863) and refined by B. H. Streeter (The Four Gospels, 1924), holds that Matthew and Luke independently used Mark and a lost sayings source called Q (German Quelle, source); it remains the majority view. The Farrer hypothesis, from Austin Farrer's essay On Dispensing with Q (1955) and defended by Michael Goulder and Mark Goodacre (The Case Against Q, 2002), keeps Mark first but has Luke using Matthew too, making Q unnecessary. The Griesbach or Two-Gospel hypothesis, from J. J. Griesbach (1789) and revived by William Farmer (The Synoptic Problem, 1964), puts Matthew first, Luke second using Matthew, and Mark as a digest of both. Luke says only that he drew on earlier accounts and eyewitnesses (1:1-2), which fits each view.

structure.title: Preface to Theophilus
structure.summary: One long, formal sentence tells how the work was made: earlier accounts, eyewitness tradition, careful investigation, and an orderly account written so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught.

structure.title: The births of John and Jesus
structure.summary: Opening “In the time of Herod king of Judea” (1:5) and written in the style of the Greek Old Testament, paired announcements, births, and songs show God keeping his promises to Israel, ending with the boy Jesus in his Father's house.

structure.title: Preparation for ministry
structure.summary: A six-part date by emperor, governor, tetrarchs, and high priests (3:1-2) opens John's preaching. Jesus is baptized and named beloved Son, his genealogy runs back to Adam, and he is tested in the wilderness.

structure.title: Ministry in Galilee
structure.summary: Marked by “Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit” (4:14), this section opens with the sermon at Nazareth and moves through healings, forgiveness, the call of disciples, and teaching, to Peter's confession and the first predictions of suffering.

structure.title: The road to Jerusalem
structure.summary: The turning point is marked in the text: “As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem” (9:51). Reminders of the destination recur (13:22, 17:11, 18:31) as Jesus teaches on discipleship, prayer, wealth, and the kingdom, with many parables found only in Luke.

structure.title: Teaching in Jerusalem
structure.summary: Marked by “He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem” (19:28), Jesus enters the city, weeps over it, clears the temple, answers his opponents, and foretells Jerusalem's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man.

structure.title: The passion
structure.summary: Jesus shares the Passover meal, prays on the Mount of Olives, is betrayed, tried before the council, Pilate, and Herod, crucified between two criminals, and buried.

structure.title: Resurrection and ascension
structure.summary: The women find the tomb empty, the risen Jesus meets disciples on the Emmaus road and in Jerusalem, opens the Scriptures to them, and is carried up into heaven, and the disciples return to the temple praising God.

themes.title: Good news to the poor
themes.body: Luke gives more attention to wealth and poverty than any other Gospel. Mary sings that God has filled the hungry and sent the rich away empty (1:53), Jesus' first sermon announces good news to the poor (4:18), his beatitudes bless the poor and pronounce woes on the rich (6:20-26), and parables like the rich fool and the rich man and Lazarus warn against trusting in possessions. Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector who gives away half his goods, shows what repentance can look like with money.

themes.title: Women and outsiders
themes.body: Women are prominent throughout Luke: Elizabeth, Mary, and Anna in the birth stories, the women who supported Jesus from their own means (8:1-3), Martha's sister Mary sitting at his feet as a disciple (10:38-42), and the women who witness the cross and first hear of the resurrection. Samaritans, whom many Jews despised, appear as the neighbor in the parable and the one grateful leper among ten. Tax collectors and sinners are welcomed at Jesus' table, which scandalizes his critics.

themes.title: Prayer
themes.body: Luke shows Jesus praying at the turning points of his life: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, before Peter's confession, at the transfiguration, in Gethsemane, and on the cross. Only Luke records the parables of the persistent friend at midnight, the persistent widow, and the Pharisee and the tax collector praying in the temple. Prayer in Luke is the ordinary posture of those who wait on God.

themes.title: The Holy Spirit
themes.body: The Spirit is active from the first chapter: John is filled with the Spirit from the womb, Mary conceives by the Spirit's power, and Elizabeth, Zechariah, and Simeon speak by the Spirit. Jesus is anointed by the Spirit at his baptism and returns to Galilee in the Spirit's power. At the end he promises the disciples power from on high, which comes at Pentecost in Acts 2.

themes.title: Salvation today, and joy
themes.body: The word today carries weight in Luke: today a Savior is born (2:11), today the Scripture is fulfilled (4:21), today salvation has come to Zacchaeus's house (19:9), today the thief will be with Jesus in paradise (23:43). Salvation is present, not only future. And it brings joy: the angels announce good news of great joy, and heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents (15:7).

themes.title: Fulfillment and divine necessity
themes.body: Luke's first sentence speaks of things fulfilled among us, and the Greek word dei, it is necessary, marks the plan of God throughout: the boy must be in his Father's house (2:49), the Son of Man must suffer (9:22), and everything written must be fulfilled (24:44). History in Luke is not random; it is the working out of what God promised in the Scriptures.

keyChapters.why: The preface explains Luke's method, and the announcements to Zechariah and Mary, with Mary's song, set out the book's themes of reversal and fulfillment.
The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, the shepherds, and Simeon's words about a light for the Gentiles anchor the good news in history and point to its reach.
Jesus' sermon at Nazareth from Isaiah 61 is his program statement for the whole ministry, and his rejection there foreshadows what follows.
The parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son show God's joy in finding the lost and expose the resentment of those who think they were never lost.
Zacchaeus's conversion and Jesus' statement that he came to seek and to save the lost lead into his entry into Jerusalem.
The empty tomb, the Emmaus road, and the ascension show the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures and sending his disciples to the nations.

text:
Luke's text is well attested and early. The oldest substantial witness is P75 (Papyrus Bodmer XIV-XV), a codex of Luke and John usually dated around AD 175 to 225, though some papyrologists place it later; it came to the Vatican Library in 2006 and 2007 and is now called the Hanna Papyrus. Its text is strikingly close to that of Codex Vaticanus, copied more than a century later. P4, fragments of Luke 1 to 6 in Paris found in the binding of a later codex of Philo, is also early; T. C. Skeat argued it came from the same codex as the Matthew fragments P64 and P67, though that is disputed. P45 (the Chester Beatty papyrus, third century) preserves parts of all four Gospels and Acts. The fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, the fifth-century Alexandrinus and Washingtonianus, and early Latin, Syriac, and Coptic translations fill out the picture.

Luke also has a distinctive textual problem. Codex Bezae (fifth century) and the Old Latin carry a Western text of Luke and Acts, fuller in Acts and at several points shorter in Luke. Westcott and Hort (1881) judged some of Bezae's shorter readings in Luke 22 and 24 original and called them Western non-interpolations; most editors now keep the longer text. So English Bibles differ. The prayer from the cross, ‘Father, forgive them’ (23:34), is missing from P75, Vaticanus, and the first hand of Bezae, and modern Bibles print it with a note or in brackets. The angel and the sweat like drops of blood (22:43-44) are absent from P75 and Vaticanus but present in Sinaiticus and Bezae. The longer account of the Last Supper (22:19b-20) is missing only from Bezae and some Latin and Syriac witnesses. The Lord's Prayer in Luke (11:2-4) is shorter in the earliest manuscripts than the King James Version, which reflects later copyists filling it out from Matthew 6. The angels' song in 2:14 differs by one letter between ‘goodwill toward men’ and ‘people of his good pleasure’. In the story of the woman caught in adultery, one family of manuscripts places it after Luke 21:38 instead of in John.

The oldest evidence for Luke comes from Marcion of Sinope, who broke with the church at Rome around AD 144 and used a single Gospel, without an author's name, closely related to Luke but shorter: it lacked chapters 1 and 2 and began with Jesus coming down to Capernaum in the fifteenth year of Tiberius. It survives only through its opponents, chiefly Tertullian (Against Marcion, book 4) and Epiphanius (Panarion 42). Those writers, and Adolf von Harnack's reconstruction (1921), treat it as Marcion's cut-down Luke, edited to remove what tied Jesus to Israel's God. John Knox (Marcion and the New Testament, 1942) proposed that canonical Luke was instead expanded from an earlier gospel that Marcion also used, and Joseph Tyson (2006) developed a version of that view. Matthias Klinghardt (2015) and Markus Vinzent (2014) argued that Marcion's Gospel came first, and Jason BeDuhn (The First New Testament, 2013) that it was an older text Marcion adopted. Dieter Roth's critical reconstruction (The Text of Marcion's Gospel, 2015), now the standard, shows how much of that Gospel is uncertain; most scholars still conclude that Marcion edited Luke.
reception:
Luke was read as the Gospel of Paul's companion from the second century. Justin Martyr drew on its birth story, Marcion's use of it forced the church to defend it as one of four, and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.11.8) gave it the calf among the four living creatures of Revelation 4 because it begins with Zechariah the priest at the altar; Jerome, in the preface to his commentary on Matthew, kept the calf or ox for Luke, and the winged ox marks Luke on lecterns and in manuscripts such as the Book of Kells. Origen preached on it at Caesarea, and thirty-nine of his homilies survive in Jerome's Latin translation. Ambrose of Milan's Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke (about 387), ten books drawn from his sermons, is the fullest Latin patristic commentary on Luke. Cyril of Alexandria's 156 homilies on Luke survive mainly in a Syriac translation brought to England from the Egyptian desert in the 1840s. Bede wrote a commentary on it in eighth-century Northumbria, and Bonaventure and Thomas Aquinas (in his Catena Aurea) carried it through the Middle Ages.

Luke's hymns entered the church's daily prayer: the Benedictus at the morning office, the Magnificat at evening prayer, and the Nunc Dimittis at Compline, a pattern the Book of Common Prayer (1549) kept in Morning and Evening Prayer. The Ave Maria and the Angelus draw on Luke 1, and the Gloria in excelsis on Luke 2:14. The church year follows Luke through Advent and Christmas, the Annunciation on 25 March, the Visitation, and the Presentation on 2 February (Candlemas). From the sixth century (Theodore Lector, around 530) a legend held that Luke painted the Virgin, which made him the patron of painters and underlies Rogier van der Weyden's Saint Luke Drawing the Virgin (about 1435 to 1440). Luke's parables gave European art the Good Samaritan and Rembrandt's Return of the Prodigal Son (late 1660s), and his birth story gave music Bach's Magnificat (1723) and Christmas Oratorio (1734), Handel's Messiah (1742), and countless carols.

Modern criticism made Luke a theologian as well as a historian. Henry Cadbury studied its style and making (1920, 1927); Hans Conzelmann (1954) read it as a theology of salvation history written to cope with the delay of Christ's return; and the commentaries of I. Howard Marshall (1978), Joseph Fitzmyer (1981 and 1985), Luke Timothy Johnson (1991), Joel Green (1997), and François Bovon (2002 to 2013) set the modern standard. Liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez made Luke's good news to the poor central to their reading, while feminist scholars have debated whether Luke honors women or confines them: Jane Schaberg, writing on Luke in The Women's Bible Commentary (1992), argued that it models silent, supporting women, and Turid Karlsen Seim (The Double Message, 1994) found in Luke-Acts both real prominence and real restraint. Jewish readers have asked how Luke's positive picture of Jewish piety in its first chapters fits its sharp words about Israel's leaders later; Amy-Jill Levine and Ben Witherington III wrote a commentary together (2018), a Jewish and a Christian scholar in conversation, that treats these questions and the book's use in Christian anti-Judaism openly.

furtherReading.author: N. T. Wright
furtherReading.title: Luke for Everyone
furtherReading.note: Short passages with a fresh translation and warm, historically informed reflection; an easy place for a newcomer to begin.

furtherReading.author: Michael Wilcock
furtherReading.title: The Message of Luke
furtherReading.note: A clear evangelical exposition that follows the shape of Luke's narrative and its Old Testament roots, written with preaching in view.

furtherReading.author: Joel B. Green
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.series: New International Commentary on the New Testament
furtherReading.note: Reads Luke as a unified narrative in its first-century social world; strong on the book's theology of salvation and its concern for the marginal.

furtherReading.author: Darrell L. Bock
furtherReading.title: Luke
furtherReading.series: Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament
furtherReading.note: A thorough two-volume evangelical commentary (1994 and 1996), careful on the Greek, historical questions, and the views of other interpreters.

furtherReading.author: Luke Timothy Johnson
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.note: A Roman Catholic literary reading that attends to how Luke tells the story and to its prophetic pattern.

furtherReading.author: Amy-Jill Levine and Ben Witherington III
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.note: A Jewish and a Christian scholar comment together, showing where they agree and differ and how Luke has been used and misused.

furtherReading.author: Arthur A. Just Jr., editor
furtherReading.title: Luke
furtherReading.note: Selections from Origen, Ambrose, Cyril of Alexandria, Bede, and other early interpreters, arranged passage by passage.

furtherReading.author: Joseph A. Fitzmyer
furtherReading.title: The Gospel According to Luke
furtherReading.note: A landmark two-volume critical commentary (1981 and 1985) by a Jesuit scholar, with a long introduction to Luke's sources, theology, and Greek.

furtherReading.author: François Bovon
furtherReading.title: Luke
furtherReading.note: A three-volume historical-critical commentary (2002 to 2013) by a Swiss Protestant scholar, rich in the history of interpretation.

furtherReading.author: I. Howard Marshall
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.note: A detailed commentary on the Greek text, strong on Luke as historian and theologian.

furtherReading.author: Raymond E. Brown
furtherReading.title: The Birth of the Messiah
furtherReading.note: The standard study of the infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke, updated in 1993; indispensable for Luke 1 and 2.

furtherReading.author: Loveday Alexander
furtherReading.title: The Preface to Luke's Gospel
furtherReading.series: Society for New Testament Studies Monograph Series
furtherReading.note: Compares Luke 1:1-4 and Acts 1:1 with ancient prefaces and argues that Luke's closest models are Greek technical treatises.

furtherReading.author: Mark Goodacre
furtherReading.title: The Case Against Q
furtherReading.note: The fullest modern case for the Farrer hypothesis, that Luke used Mark and Matthew; read with a defense of the Two-Source view for balance.

parts.body:
Luke is the third of the four Gospels, the books that tell the story of Jesus. It has 24 chapters and is the longest of the four. It is also the first half of a two-part work. The second half is the book of Acts, which tells what happened after Jesus rose.

Luke begins like no other Gospel. Before any story, he writes one long, careful sentence about how he made his book. Many people had already written accounts. He has looked into everything from the beginning, and now he writes an orderly account for a man called Theophilus, “so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught” (1:4).

Then the story opens in the temple in Jerusalem, with an old priest and a promise. It moves through the births of John the Baptist and Jesus, Jesus' work in Galilee, a long walk to Jerusalem, and his death, rising and going up to heaven.

Luke's Gospel is full of people others passed over: the poor, widows, the sick, Samaritans, tax collectors, women, sinners. Many of its best-loved stories are found only here: the shepherds at the manger, the Good Samaritan, the lost son, Zacchaeus in the tree, the thief on the cross, the road to Emmaus. Jesus sums up the whole book in one line: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10).

It ends where it began, in the temple, with the disciples “praising God continually” (24:53).

parts.h: Who wrote it, and how we know
parts.body:
The book does not name its writer. The name Luke comes from the early church, and the evidence comes in three kinds: what Paul's letters say, what the book of Acts suggests, and what early Christian writers report.

Paul's letters. Paul names a Luke three times. He sends greetings from “Luke, the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). He lists Luke among “my fellow workers” (Philemon 24). And near the end of his life, in prison, he writes, “Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). So a Luke was a close friend of Paul, a travel companion, and a doctor.

The ‘we’ passages. Acts is written mostly about ‘they’. But in a few places the story suddenly says ‘we’: from Troas to Philippi (Acts 16:10-17), from Philippi to Jerusalem (Acts 20:5 to 21:18), and on the sea voyage to Rome (Acts 27:1 to 28:16). The plainest reading is that the writer was there, travelling with Paul. Some scholars think the writer used someone else's travel diary, or that ‘we’ was a way of telling sea stories. Others have answered that no such custom has been clearly shown. Most who accept the plain reading look for a companion of Paul who is not named in Acts, and Luke fits.

The early writers. Around AD 180, Irenaeus, a bishop in Gaul (modern France), wrote that Luke, the companion of Paul, set down in a book the gospel Paul preached (Against Heresies 3.1.1). Later in the same work he uses the ‘we’ passages to argue that Luke was Paul's constant companion (3.14.1). A Latin list of accepted books, called the Muratorian fragment, also names Luke the physician as the writer, says Paul took him along, and says Luke did not see the Lord in the flesh. Most date it to the late second century; a few scholars argue it is from the fourth. No other name was ever attached to this Gospel.

‘The beloved physician’. In 1882 W. K. Hobart argued that Luke's Greek is full of medical words, which proved a doctor wrote it. Henry Cadbury answered him, from 1919 on. He showed that educated Greek writers who were not doctors used the same words, and that ancient doctors had hardly any special vocabulary of their own. Most scholars now agree with Cadbury. So the medical words do not prove the case. The case rests on Paul's letters, the ‘we’ passages and the early church's memory.

Was Luke a Gentile? A Gentile is someone who is not Jewish. In Colossians 4:10-11 Paul names three men and says, “These are the only Jews among my fellow workers.” Luke is greeted after that, in verse 14. So many readers have concluded that Luke was a Gentile, and the only Gentile writer in the New Testament. Others reply that the Greek phrase behind ‘Jews’ there may mean a narrower group, the strictest keepers of the law, and that Luke's deep knowledge of the Jewish Scriptures fits a Jewish writer, or a Gentile who had long worshipped with Jews. Both views have careful defenders.

parts.h: One work in two volumes, for Theophilus
parts.body:
Acts begins, “In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). The ‘first book’ is Luke. The same man is named at the start of both. The same writer, the same style and the same themes run through both. Luke ends with Jesus going up to heaven, and Acts begins by telling it again. Henry Cadbury's study The Making of Luke-Acts (1927) treated the two as one project, and scholars often write ‘Luke-Acts’ for the pair.

Read together, the two books make one long story. Luke moves toward Jerusalem. Acts moves out from Jerusalem ‘to the ends of the earth’, and ends with Paul preaching in Rome. Things begun in the first book are finished in the second: the promise of the Holy Spirit (Luke 24:49) is kept at Pentecost (Acts 2), and the word to ‘all nations’ (Luke 24:47) reaches them.

In the old copies, though, the two books did not travel together. Luke sits with the other Gospels; Acts usually came before the letters.

Who was Theophilus? His name is Greek and means ‘friend of God’ or ‘loved by God’. Luke calls him “most excellent Theophilus” (1:3), and in Acts the same title is used for the Roman governors Felix and Festus (Acts 24:3, 26:25). So there are several views.

Many think he was a real man of rank, perhaps a patron. Writers in the Roman world often dedicated a book to a supporter who paid for copies to be made and passed around. Others think he was a believer who had been taught the faith and needed firm ground under it, which fits 1:4. A few have suggested the name stands for every reader who loves God. Luke does not say more, and no one knows for sure.

parts.h: The opening sentence: what kind of history
parts.body:
Luke 1:1-4 is one long sentence in polished Greek. Nothing like it opens Matthew, Mark or John. Read it slowly, because Luke is telling you how to read the rest.

Many people, he says, have already written accounts of “the things that have been fulfilled among us” (1:1). The word ‘fulfilled’ matters. These are not just events; they are promises coming true.

The accounts were “handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word” (1:2). Luke does not claim to be an eyewitness himself. He claims to stand close to those who were.

He has “carefully investigated everything from the beginning” (1:3). He has done the work of checking.

And he writes “an orderly account” (1:3). Orderly does not always mean in strict date order. It means arranged with care, so the story makes sense.

Why? “So that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught” (1:4). Theophilus already believes. Luke writes so his faith can stand on solid ground.

What kind of writing does this sound like? Greek historians often opened with a note about their sources and method, and many scholars think Luke wanted to be read alongside them. Loveday Alexander, in The Preface to Luke's Gospel (1993), argued that the closest matches are the short prefaces of Greek technical and scientific handbooks, written by working men for practical readers. Others think the line between those two kinds of preface is less sharp than she drew it. On any view, Luke is claiming something plain: this is an account of real events, gathered from people who saw them, checked and set in order.

Luke gives no date. Since Acts calls Luke ‘my first book’, Luke was written first, and the two are usually dated together. The big question, as with Matthew, is whether Luke wrote before or after AD 70, when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and its temple.

The case for after 70. Most scholars date Luke somewhere around AD 80 to 90. Their reasons are these. First, most think Luke used Mark, which is usually dated to the late 60s or about 70. Second, Luke's form of Jesus' warnings about Jerusalem is very concrete. Mark speaks of a coming horror; Luke says, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near” (21:20), and speaks of enemies building a barricade around the city (19:43). Many read that as written by someone who knew how the siege of 70 went.

The case for before 70. A smaller group of scholars, including John A. T. Robinson in Redating the New Testament (1976), date Luke and Acts in the early 60s. Their strongest point is the end of Acts. Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome for “two full years” (Acts 28:30), still waiting for his trial. It never says how the trial ended, or that Paul died, or that Jerusalem fell. If Luke knew those things, why stop there? On this view he stopped because events had reached his own day. They add that siege language was common in Israel's prophets, so Luke 21:20 needs no hindsight.

The other side answers that Acts ends where it does on purpose. The story was always heading for Rome, and its last words show Paul preaching without hindrance: “Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God” (Acts 28:31). The goal is reached; the book is done.

A few scholars place Luke and Acts even later, early in the second century. That is a minority view.

Each case has able defenders, and the site does not settle the question. Nothing in the faith hangs on the year.

Luke tells us he used earlier accounts and what eyewitnesses handed down (1:1-2). Laying the Gospels side by side shows three kinds of material in Luke.

Material shared with Mark. Much of Luke follows Mark, often in the same order and with many of the same words: the healings in Galilee, the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the last week in Jerusalem. Most scholars think Luke had Mark's Gospel in front of him.

Material shared with Matthew but not Mark. Luke and Matthew share many sayings of Jesus that Mark does not have, such as the Lord's Prayer and the blessings that open Jesus' great sermon. How did that happen? As on Matthew's page, the answers are hypotheses, careful guesses from the evidence. The most common view is that Matthew and Luke each used Mark and also a lost collection of sayings that scholars call Q, from the German word Quelle, ‘source’. A second view, argued by Austin Farrer in 1955 and by Mark Goodacre in The Case Against Q (2002), has no Q: Luke used Matthew as well as Mark. A third view puts Matthew first and Luke second, with Mark drawing on both. Each has able defenders, and the site does not settle it.

Material only in Luke. A large part of Luke is found in no other Gospel. Scholars sometimes call it ‘L’, a label for Luke's own material, not the name of a known document. Where did it come from? Luke's preface points to eyewitnesses. Some have noticed that the birth stories are told from Mary's side, and that Luke twice says Mary kept these things in her heart (2:19, 2:51). Others think Luke gathered stories from many people over many years. We do not know his sources by name.

What matters most is what Luke says himself: he did not invent his story. He received it and checked it.

Luke's story moves toward one city. The outline at the top of this page draws it as a diagram you can tap. Here it is in words.

The opening (1:1-4). The preface to Theophilus.

The births (1:5 to 2:52). Two births are announced and told side by side, John's and Jesus'. Each has an angel, a song and a note on how the child grew. At the end the boy Jesus is found in the temple.

Getting ready (3:1 to 4:13). John preaches in the wilderness. Jesus is baptized, his family line is traced back to Adam, and he is tested in the desert.

Galilee (4:14 to 9:50). It begins with Jesus' sermon in his home town of Nazareth, where he reads from Isaiah and is nearly thrown off a cliff. Then come healings, the calling of disciples, teaching and the question of who he is.

The road to Jerusalem (9:51 to 19:27). This is the turning point: “As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem” (9:51). Luke reminds the reader again and again where Jesus is heading (13:22, 17:11, 18:31). This long middle section holds much of what only Luke has: the Good Samaritan, the lost sheep, coin and son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus. It is less a map of the route than a school for disciples on the way.

Jerusalem (19:28 to 24:53). Jesus enters the city, weeps over it, clears the temple and teaches there each day. Then come the last supper, his arrest, his trials before the council, Pilate and Herod, his death and burial, the empty tomb, the walk to Emmaus, and his going up to heaven from near Bethany.

The book begins and ends in the temple. In between, everything leans toward Jerusalem, where God's promises will be kept.

Good news to the poor. In his first sermon Jesus reads Isaiah: “He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor” (4:18). Luke uses the words ‘poor’ and ‘rich’ more than any other Gospel. His Jesus is born in a feeding trough and visited by shepherds.

The great reversal. Mary sings that God “has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble” (1:52). Luke's Jesus blesses the poor and pronounces woes on the rich (6:20-26). The last become first; the proud are humbled.

The lost and the outsider. Tax collectors, sinners, Samaritans and lepers keep turning up, and Jesus welcomes them. Chapter 15 gives three stories in a row about something lost and found.

Women. Luke names women again and again: Elizabeth, Mary, Anna, the widow of Nain, the woman who weeps on Jesus' feet, Mary and Martha, and the women who travel with Jesus and support him from their own means (8:1-3). Women are the first to find the empty tomb (24:1-10).

The Holy Spirit. The Spirit fills Elizabeth, Zechariah and Simeon, comes on Jesus at his baptism, and leads him into the desert and back to Galilee. At the end Jesus promises the Spirit's power (24:49), and Acts tells how it came.

Prayer. Luke shows Jesus praying at his baptism (3:21), before he chooses the twelve (6:12), when he is transfigured (9:29) and on the cross. Parables about prayer are found only here (11:5-8, 18:1-14).

Joy. The angel brings ‘good news of great joy’ (2:10). Heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents (15:7). The book ends “with great joy” (24:52).

The table. Jesus is often at a meal: with tax collectors, with Pharisees, with Martha and Mary, with the crowd, with his disciples, and at Emmaus, where he is known “in the breaking of the bread” (24:35).

‘Today’. Luke uses the word for the moment God's promise arrives: a Savior born today (2:11), Scripture fulfilled today (4:21), salvation come to Zacchaeus today (19:9), paradise today (23:43).

Salvation for all nations. Simeon calls the child “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:32). Luke traces Jesus' line back to Adam, the father of everyone (3:38). The last commission is for ‘all nations’ (24:47).

Jerusalem and the temple. The story starts with a priest at the altar, keeps heading for the city, and ends with the disciples in the temple courts. God keeps his promises to Israel first, in Israel's own house.

A large part of Luke is found in no other Gospel. Here are some of the best-known pieces.

The songs. Luke's first two chapters hold four songs that the church has sung ever since, each named from its first words in Latin. The Magnificat is Mary's song (1:46-55): “My soul magnifies the Lord.” The Benedictus is Zechariah's (1:68-79): “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel.” The Gloria is the angels' (2:14): “Glory to God in the highest.” The Nunc Dimittis is Simeon's (2:29-32): “You now dismiss Your servant in peace.”

The birth stories from Mary's side: the angel Gabriel's visit to Zechariah and to Mary, the shepherds, Simeon and Anna, and the boy Jesus in the temple.

The parables. The Good Samaritan (10:25-37). The friend at midnight (11:5-8). The rich fool (12:13-21). The lost coin and the lost son (15:8-32). The shrewd manager (16:1-9). The rich man and Lazarus (16:19-31). The widow and the unjust judge (18:1-8). The Pharisee and the tax collector (18:9-14).

The people. The widow of Nain, whose only son Jesus raises (7:11-17). The sinful woman who weeps at his feet (7:36-50). Mary and Martha (10:38-42). The ten lepers, of whom only the Samaritan comes back to say thank you (17:11-19). Zacchaeus, the short tax collector up a tree (19:1-10).

At the cross and after. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem (19:41-44). He prays “Father, forgive them” (23:34). He promises the dying criminal, “today you will be with Me in Paradise” (23:43). And on the road to Emmaus he walks with two sad disciples who do not know him until he breaks bread (24:13-35).

Without Luke, the church would not have most of its Christmas story, and some of the stories it loves best.

Luke quotes the Old Testament less often by name than Matthew does. But it sounds through his book from the first page.

The sound of chapters 1 and 2. After the polished preface, Luke's Greek changes. The birth stories read like the Greek translation of the Old Testament, called the Septuagint, which the first churches used. An old childless couple recalls Abraham and Sarah. Gabriel is the angel of the book of Daniel. Mary's song echoes Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2. Most scholars think Luke chose this style on purpose, to show that Israel's story is starting up again. Some think he was using older Hebrew or Aramaic sources. Either way, the first readers would have heard their Bible in it.

Isaiah 61 at Nazareth. Jesus' first sermon in Luke is a reading from the scroll of Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor” (4:18-19, from Isaiah 61:1-2 with a line from Isaiah 58:6). Then he sits down and says, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21). The rest of the Gospel shows him doing what he read.

He stops before Isaiah's next words, “the day of our God's vengeance” (Isaiah 61:2). Many readers have noticed this. In Luke this is a time of favour first.

The whole Scripture. At the end, the risen Jesus tells his disciples, “Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (24:44). Those are the three parts of the Jewish Bible. On the Emmaus road, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself” (24:27). Luke's claim is not that a few verses point to Jesus, but that the whole story does.

parts.h: Luke and the history of his day
parts.body:
Luke ties his story to the wider world more than any other Gospel. He names emperors, governors and kings. That makes his account easier to check, and in one place it raises a real difficulty.

The rulers of 3:1-2. Luke dates the start of John's preaching with six names: “the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas” (3:1-2). A tetrarch was a ruler of part of a kingdom. Most count Tiberius's fifteenth year as AD 28 or 29; some count from an earlier date, which gives about AD 26. Pilate governed Judea from about 26 to 36. In 1961 a stone found at Caesarea on the coast was seen to bear his name and the title ‘prefect of Judea’.

Lysanias was once called a mistake. Josephus speaks of a Lysanias who ruled a nearby land and was put to death about 36 BC, long before. But an inscription found at Abila, the chief town of Abilene, records a gift by a freed slave of ‘Lysanias the tetrarch’. Most date it to the reign of Tiberius, though its exact date is debated. So there seems to have been a later Lysanias, as Luke says.

The census of 2:1-2. Here the difficulty is real. Luke says Joseph went to Bethlehem because of a census ordered by Augustus, “the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria” (2:2). Luke and Matthew both place the birth while Herod the Great was alive, and most date Herod's death to 4 BC. But Quirinius became governor of Syria in AD 6, about ten years later. That year Judea came under direct Roman rule, and the Jewish historian Josephus describes the census Quirinius took then. No writer outside Luke tells of a Roman census in Herod's kingdom.

Several explanations have been offered. Many scholars conclude that Luke joined the famous census of AD 6 to the time of the birth by mistake. Others think Quirinius held an earlier command in Syria; an inscription found near Tivoli in Italy speaks of an unnamed official who governed Syria a second time, and some read it as Quirinius while others assign it to another man. Others note that the Greek word for ‘first’ can sometimes mean ‘before’, giving ‘this census took place before Quirinius was governor’; most experts in Greek grammar find that reading strained. Others point out that Tertullian, writing around 200, tied a census in Judea to Sentius Saturninus, who governed Syria a few years before Herod died. And some suggest a count begun under Herod and finished later. Luke knows the famous census of AD 6 well (Acts 5:37), which some take as a sign he was not confused about it.

The question is about a date. It does not touch the confession that Jesus was born as a real man in real history. These notes do not settle it.

Luke's Gospel begins and ends in the Jewish temple. Its first scenes are full of faithful Jews: Zechariah and Elizabeth, ‘righteous in the sight of God’; Mary and Joseph, who keep the law of Moses; old Simeon, waiting for ‘the consolation of Israel’; Anna, praying in the temple night and day. Jesus is circumcised, presented in the temple and taken up to Jerusalem for Passover. His first followers are all Jews. After he rises, they return to Jerusalem and are “praising God continually in the temple” (24:53).

Luke also tells of conflict. Jesus' own town tries to kill him (4:29). The chief priests and leaders plot against him, and some in the crowd call for his death. Luke is just as clear that many in Jerusalem grieve. A great crowd follows him to the cross, including women who mourn and wail for him (23:27). The crowds go home beating their chests (23:48).

Over the centuries, Christians have misused Gospel passages to blame the whole Jewish people for Jesus' death, and called Jews ‘Christ-killers’. That reading fed contempt, expulsion and murder. It is wrong, and the site rejects it plainly, as on the pages for Mark, Matthew and John. Luke's own second book says that Herod and Pontius Pilate “conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel” against Jesus (Acts 4:27): Jew and Gentile, ruler and crowd, together. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) taught that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and many Protestant churches have said the same.

‘Father, forgive them’. Only Luke gives this prayer from the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (23:34). The line is missing from some of the oldest copies of Luke, including a papyrus called P75, copied around AD 200, Codex Vaticanus from the 300s, and Codex Bezae as first written. It is present in Codex Sinaiticus as first written and in most later copies. Scholars are divided. Some think it was added from an early story about Jesus. Others think some scribes left it out because they could not bear the thought of the Jews who rejected Jesus being forgiven. Many modern Bibles print it with a note or in brackets. Stephen, dying in Acts, prays in the same way: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60).

Luke does not give a verdict on the Jewish people. He tells of a Jewish Messiah, welcomed and refused by his own as prophets had been before, who prays for those who kill him.

No Gospel says more about money than Luke. It is worth being honest about how hard his words are.

Mary sings that God “has sent the rich away empty” (1:53). Jesus says, “Woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort” (6:24). He tells of a farmer who builds bigger barns and dies that night (12:16-21). He tells of a rich man who feasted every day while a poor man named Lazarus lay at his gate, and the rich man ends in torment (16:19-31). He tells a ruler to sell everything and give to the poor, and says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God (18:22-25).

There are two easy ways out, and Luke closes both.

The first is to make money a sign of God's blessing, so that the rich are the most blessed and the poor must lack faith. This is often called the prosperity gospel. Luke turns it upside down. In his book, wealth is more often a danger than a reward.

The second is to despise the rich as if they were beyond God's reach. Luke does not do that either. Women of means support Jesus from what they own (8:3). Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector, is welcomed, and salvation comes to his house when he gives half his goods to the poor and repays those he cheated four times over (19:8-9). Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the Council, gives Jesus an honourable burial (23:50-53). When the disciples ask, “Who then can be saved?”, Jesus answers, “What is impossible with man is possible with God” (18:26-27).

Luke's point is not that being poor makes anyone good, or that being rich makes anyone bad. It is that money is a rival master, “You cannot serve both God and money” (16:13), and that God has a special care for those who have nothing. Every reader, rich or poor by the world's standard, is asked where their treasure is.

parts.h: How the church has read Luke
parts.body:
From the second century, Luke was read as the Gospel of Paul's companion. Irenaeus defended its place among the four Gospels against teachers, Marcion among them, who would not accept all of it.

Luke's songs entered the church's daily prayer. In the church's old daily round of prayer, the Benedictus was sung at morning prayer, the Magnificat at evening prayer and the Nunc Dimittis at night prayer. The Book of Common Prayer kept them in Morning and Evening Prayer, and many churches still sing them every day. The angels' song became the Gloria of Christian worship, and Gabriel's greeting and Elizabeth's words to Mary (1:28, 1:42) became the opening of the Hail Mary.

In the art of the church each Gospel writer has a symbol, taken from the four living creatures of Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4. Irenaeus gave Luke the calf, because his Gospel begins with Zechariah the priest at the altar, where calves were offered. Jerome, in 398, kept the calf for Luke for the same reason. So in old Bibles and church windows Luke is shown with an ox, often with wings.

Luke's stories gave the world some of its most familiar words and pictures. ‘Good Samaritan’ became a name for anyone who helps a stranger. Rembrandt painted the lost son's return, and much of the church's Christmas music sets Luke 2.

Above all, Luke gave the church its picture of a Savior who goes looking for the lost, eats with sinners and prays for his enemies.

hard.line: The census ‘while Quirinius was governor of Syria’. A real historical difficulty, the main explanations, and why the notes take no side.
Jesus reminds his home town that Elijah and Elisha were sent to outsiders, and they try to kill him. Why did that make them so angry?
‘Blessed are you who are poor’ and ‘woe to you who are rich’. Does Luke mean money, or the heart? Both, and how they fit.
‘I have come to ignite a fire on the earth’ and to bring division. How does that fit the Prince of Peace?
Hate your father and mother? What the word meant in Jesus' way of speaking, and what it still demands.
The master praises a dishonest manager. What is being praised, and what is not?
The rich man and Lazarus. Is this a picture of the life to come, a parable about wealth, or both?
Is the kingdom of God ‘within you’ or ‘in your midst’? What the Greek allows.
‘Buy a sword’, and then ‘That is enough’. Was Jesus arming his disciples?
The angel and the sweat like drops of blood. Missing from some of the oldest copies; what that means.
‘Father, forgive them’. A prayer missing from some early copies, and why scholars are divided.
‘Today you will be with Me in Paradise’. What did Jesus promise the dying thief?

words.line: Greek sōtēr. One who rescues. The angels call Jesus ‘a Savior’ (2:11); Roman cities gave the same title to the emperor.
Greek euangelizomai, to bring good news, the root of ‘gospel’ and ‘evangelist’. Luke's favourite verb for preaching (4:18, 8:1).
Greek sēmeron. Luke's word for the moment God's promise arrives (2:11, 4:21, 19:9, 23:43).
God's rule, God putting the world right. It comes near in Jesus (10:9) and is ‘in your midst’ (17:21).
Greek metanoia, a change of mind and life. Preached by John (3:3) and sent to all nations (24:47).
Those who have wandered from God, like a sheep, a coin or a son (chapter 15). Jesus came to seek them (19:10).
In Luke, people with little money and little power, often the ones who know they need God (4:18, 6:20).
God's own Spirit, who fills people to speak, rests on Jesus, and is promised to the disciples (3:22, 24:49).
Greek dei, it is necessary. Luke's word for God's plan: the Son of Man must suffer and rise (9:22, 24:7).
Jesus' favourite name for himself, from Daniel 7:13; one who serves, suffers and will come in glory (19:10, 21:27).
The man Luke writes to; the name means ‘friend of God’ (1:3, Acts 1:1).
A Persian word for a garden; used for the place of the righteous dead with God (23:43).
A ruler of part of a kingdom under Rome, such as Herod Antipas in Galilee (3:1, 3:19).

timeline.what: Herod the Great rules Judea as king under Rome. Luke begins ‘in the time of Herod king of Judea’ (1:5).
Augustus is the first Roman emperor. Luke names his decree for a census (2:1).
Cities in the province of Asia call Augustus's birthday the beginning of good news for the world.
Jesus is born in Bethlehem, while Herod is still alive (1:5, 2:4-7).
Judea comes under direct Roman rule. Quirinius, governor of Syria, takes a census (Acts 5:37).
Herod Antipas rules Galilee. He imprisons John and questions Jesus (3:19-20, 23:7-12).
Tiberius becomes emperor. Luke dates John's preaching by his fifteenth year (3:1).
Pontius Pilate governs Judea. He tries Jesus and sends him to Herod (23:1-25).
The fifteenth year of Tiberius on the usual count: John preaches and baptizes Jesus (3:1-22).
The two dates most often proposed for the crucifixion.
The risen Jesus is carried up into heaven near Bethany (24:50-51; Acts 1:3).
Paul under guard in Rome for two years, where Acts ends (Acts 28:30).
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and its temple.
The date most scholars give for Luke. A smaller group argues for the early 60s.
Irenaeus writes that Luke, Paul's companion, set down the gospel Paul preached.
The papyrus P75 is copied; it holds most of Luke and John.
Jerome gives Luke the calf as his symbol, because he begins with Zechariah the priest.

map.name: Capernaum
map.line: A fishing town on the north shore of the lake. Jesus teaches in its synagogue, and heals a centurion's servant here (7:1-10).

map.name: Nazareth
map.line: A small village in the hills of Galilee. Gabriel comes to Mary here; Jesus grows up here and is nearly thrown off its hill (4:29).

map.name: Nain
map.line: A village on the slope of the hill of Moreh, a few miles from Nazareth. Jesus raises a widow's only son (7:11-17).

map.name: Samaritan villages
map.line: The land between Galilee and Judea. A Samaritan village refuses Jesus (9:52); a Samaritan leper comes back to thank him (17:16). Placed roughly.

map.name: Jericho
map.line: An oasis town near the Jordan, the last stop before the climb to Jerusalem. A blind man is healed and Zacchaeus climbs a tree here (19:1-10).

map.name: Emmaus
map.line: Where two disciples know the risen Jesus at supper (24:13-35). Its site is uncertain: Nicopolis, Abu Ghosh, El-Qubeibeh and Motza are all proposed. Placed roughly.

map.name: Jerusalem
map.line: The city of the temple, where the book begins and ends. Jesus sets his face toward it (9:51), weeps over it, dies outside its walls and rises.

map.name: Bethany
map.line: A village on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem. From near here Jesus blesses his disciples and is carried up into heaven (24:50-51).

map.name: Bethlehem
map.line: David's town, a few miles south of Jerusalem. Jesus is born here and laid in a manger; shepherds come from the fields nearby (2:4-20).
